narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average ranking of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your first-year ranking had a smaller but still negative effect for the same reason; you again placed in the lowest decile while accepted students averaged near the middle.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.40 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, so the model saw this as a positive sign that slightly increased your chances of passing. However, this encouraging factor was not strong enough to outweigh the impact of your low class rankings.

The model also noted your LSAT score of 29, well below the 37 average of accepted students, and your middle family income bracket, which is common but not among the highest-earning groups that tend to perform better.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger readiness. Consider targeted bar-prep resources or a post-baccalaureate program before reapplying. (248 words)
